title: What a design document here must satisfy
text:
Five documents have been through adversarial review in this project. All five were blocked: P01v2, P02, P03, P05 and P06, each by two reviewers from different providers, each on evidenced fatal findings that were checked against primary source and found correct. The findings are not evenly spread. The same mistakes recur under different names, and every item below names the document that produced it.
This follows the sibling project ITC-open-problems/studies/DESIGN-STANDARD.md, whose governing rule is kept unchanged: the difference between a design and a protocol is a set of computed numbers. That standard was written after its program repeated its own mistakes. This one is written for the same reason, at the point where outcome peeking had happened twice and extraction artifacts three times.
A design that satisfies this list is still a design. It becomes a protocol when its probes have run and their numbers are written in, and it is registered only when the probes are complete, the validation gates have passed, and two reviews are attached.



R01 fitted its model against a one-page proposal. P01v2 was written to fix that and then its own probe P4 tabulated the primary outcome by arm on the confirmatory sample, a crude odds ratio of 5.6, before the document called itself confirmatory. Both reviewers found it independently.
Required. Probes measure the frame and the instruments only. A probe that cross-tabulates the primary outcome by the primary exposure on the analysis sample is forbidden. If an instrument must be piloted on real outcomes, the pilot draws a slice that is removed from the analysis sample before the probe runs, and the removal is recorded.



P01v2’s extractor missed statements that sat in <body> and discarded xlink:href, so a real GitHub deposit graded as declarative. Five of P05’s seven “hard 404s” were URLs cut short by a regex over flattened text; the deposits were fine.
Required. Where a validated tool exists, use it: rtransparency for transparency indicators, rfair for FAIR assessment and identifier parsing. Both are maintained by this project’s author and that is disclosed in every design that uses them. Identifiers come from structured markup (ext-link/@xlink:href, pub-id[@pub-id-type='doi']) or from rfair::id_parse, never from a regex over text with the markup stripped. A hand-written extractor needs an audit in both directions before use: what it misses and what it invents.



rtransparency::rt_accuracy reports sensitivity 0.765 and specificity 0.990 for data sharing. A quarter of real sharing is missed. That is a design fact, not a footnote.
Required. Any design using a detector with known sensitivity and specificity states them and specifies a misclassification analysis (probabilistic bias analysis or a corrected estimator) as a preregistered sensitivity analysis. A detector with no published accuracy on the target literature, such as rt_ai_pmc, needs its own validation gate.



P06’s unit was a preprint paired with its journal version. Its probe counted any record with a repository location, primary locations included, and never established a single pair. P05’s hypothesis was about statements graded actionable; its probe sampled every non-empty statement.
Required. The probe that sizes the sample must construct the unit of analysis as defined, and report how many candidates failed construction and why.



P02 computed feasibility across two caches without applying its own eligibility criteria. P06 added 66 and 75 when three PMIDs were in both, because the frame file still held the tier A overlaps that the P01v2 probe had excluded in memory.
Required. Eligibility is applied before any feasibility number is computed. Each record is counted once, by a stated identifier, after deduplication across every source that feeds it.



P03 said excluding 2025 and 2026 would drop 76 percent of its sample; that was false for the window it named. P06 said 108 was below 80. The agenda miscounted its own documents. A probe comment asserted the unscreened rate was an upper bound when it was a lower one.
Required. Any number that appears in both code and prose is written from the code’s output. A sentence that reasons about a computed number (above, below, larger, most) is checked against the number before the document is committed.



P02 compared calendar years, so 41 same-year citations defaulted to pre-retraction. P05 read an age slope off a single cross-section and treated it as decay.
Required. Temporal ordering uses full dates, with an explicit third class for pairs that cannot be ordered. A claim about change over time needs repeated measurement of the same units or a design that identifies the slope; otherwise it is stated as a cohort difference.



P03 gated a four-category classifier on overall kappa, which does not validate the binary comparison its model uses, against a human reference standard that had no coding rubric.
Required. The validation gate is computed on the contrast that enters the model. The human reference standard has a written rubric with decision rules and worked examples, published with the design, and it is produced by the author rather than by a model.



P02 promised articles matched on journal and year and specified no ratio, no replacement rule and no handling of unmatched strata.
Required. Matching variables, ratio, with or without replacement, the treatment of unmatched units, and the weighting that follows are all stated.



P03 read zero citations as “nobody used it” when most of its 2026 zeros were articles too new to have been cited.
Required. Count outcomes that accrue over time carry exposure time or a censoring rule, and a fixed follow-up window is preferred to raw totals.



P05 claimed a gap that Federer and colleagues had already filled. A candidate for this round tested a hypothesis that PMID 36109655 had already tested in its title. The novelty log was first built on NCBI’s default date ordering, so each “top ten” was the ten newest hits.
Required. Every claim that something has not been studied shows its corpus regex and its PubMed query verbatim, run through build/lit/novelty.py with relevance ordering, and cites the log entry. A PMID cited as prior work must appear in data/lit/novelty-log.json or in the harvested corpus; tools/check_citations.py enforces this in CI and fails the build on any PMID that came from neither. The author’s own repositories and papers are checked first: a design that re-runs the author’s work with a new population is not a new design.



P01v2 computed power from a two-proportion normal approximation for a mixed model with a journal random effect, and read a confidence interval containing 1 as evidence of absence.
Required. Power or precision is computed for the specified model, by simulation where no closed form fits. A design that wants to claim absence of an effect states the equivalence margin or precision target that would license the claim.




Pin by hash. An instrument is pinned by a commit hash written into the document together with the git show command that resolves it. A prose pin (“the commit this was published in”) is not a pin.
Status says what it is. design until the probes run; protocol once their numbers are written in; blocked-by-review when review finds an unrebutted evidenced fatal flaw; agenda when public data cannot answer the question. A document is never labeled for the stage it is hoping to reach.

title: Review of P01v2: blocked
text:
What each reviewer said

chatgpt
Pinned outcome instruments demonstrably misclassify real disclosures, and validation cannot detect important extraction failures. Power and null-result interpretations also exceed what calculations establish. Frame counts and all 15 power-grid cells reproduced; no residual tier A overlap was found by PMID, DOI, or PMCID. Screening yields, human agreement, and power for the specified mixed model remain unverified. Python extractor functions were executed; R execution was blocked by read-only temporary-file restrictions, so grading was checked through source inspection and a Python translation reproducing all six P4 counts. Literature searches did not establish an exact prior study duplicating this comparison.


grok
PMID exclusion of the 205 tier A records is real. I found no leftover overlap by PMID, PMCID, DOI, or title, so the article set is not R01’s. Section 4.1 block counts match the 2026-09-16 PubMed search log, and the section 7 n’s match probes.json. The extractor is imported rather than copied. Those parts hold. The confirmatory claim does not. P3 and P4 already fetched and graded the confirmatory full-text frame by arm (95/520 versus 132/3435; crude odds ratio 5.59), and section 7 publishes both rates. That is an exposure-by-outcome look, even without glmer. Section 7 then overstates what a null can mean: the grid does not detect 1.5 in the worst cell, power is an unclustered two-proportion test rather than the mixed model, and it assumes the same screening yield in both arms. The unlabeled P6 titles are mostly clinical reviews in the comparison arm and database or resource papers in the exposed arm, so yield 0.5 is not a floor and yield is not common across arms. The written grading rule does not match grade.R, P7 is not stratified by grade, screening is unpinned, and section 13 points at R01’s analyzer, which is a different model. I looked for a published empirical test of this same topic-versus-own-statement contrast and did not find one. Cristea, Naudet, and Caquelin 2022 (PMID 35623542) is a commentary that meta-researchers should evaluate their own sharing; it is not this analysis.

title: Review of P01v2: blocked
text:
Fatal findings

F1. Outcome ascertainment confounds disclosure with publisher XML placement. Executing the pinned extractor on PMC5808091, a
Reviewer chatgpt · Section 6.1 Extraction; 9. Threats, and what happened to each
Outcome ascertainment confounds disclosure with publisher XML placement. Executing the pinned extractor on PMC5808091, an exposed article, and PMC6092896, a comparison article, returned empty statements and route ‘none’, although both contain their own repository disclosures inside

. Moving the identical sections into  in memory made extraction succeed. Their disclosures are independently visible in the metabolomics article and predatory-journal review. Excluding body content removes some false positives by introducing demonstrable false negatives. The threat is not removed.

That code searches <front> and <back> only, never <body>

What would fix it. Identify articles’ own availability statements across JATS locations while distinguishing disclosures from methods and results discussing availability. Validate extraction against complete articles across both arms and publisher formats, including records currently classified ‘none’, then freeze the corrected instrument.


F2. The document presents itself as a confirmatory protocol whose instruments were fixed before data were retrieved and whos
Reviewer grok · Section Status: protocol
The document presents itself as a confirmatory protocol whose instruments were fixed before data were retrieved and whose hypothesis has not been tested on this sample. Probes P3 and P4 already fetched PMC full text for the confirmatory frame, graded every full-text record under the pinned rule, and wrote per-arm grade counts into probes.json and p4-grades.csv. Section 7 then publishes both rates. The unscreened 2x2 is 95/520 actionable in the exposed arm versus 132/3435 in the comparison arm (odds ratio 5.59). No glmer is required for that to be a look at the hypothesis. Section 10 describes P4 as the comparison arm only; the code and the protocol text both report the exposed arm as well. The author who will adjudicate screening disagreements has seen the direction and size of the association. A confirmatory protocol cannot be written after that look.

No outcome has been analyzed under this protocol. The probes measured the frame and the instruments; they did not test the hypothesis, and no exposure-by-outcome model has been fitted on this sample.

What would fix it. Drop the confirmatory label. State that P3/P4 were an outcome-by-exposure pilot on the unscreened frame. Freeze any screening or analysis choice that could still be influenced by those rates. Do not claim that instruments were fixed before data retrieval. Register the revised protocol before P6/P7 labeling and before screening the frame.


F3. Section 1 says this is a confirmatory test with every instrument fixed before any data are retrieved. The confirmatory s
Reviewer grok · Section 1. Why this design exists
Section 1 says this is a confirmatory test with every instrument fixed before any data are retrieved. The confirmatory sample has already been retrieved, extracted, and graded. The instruments that were frozen are the R01 extractor and grading rule; the data of this study were not unseen when this page was written. The same commit that pins the code also ran the probes.

This specifies a confirmatory test of the same hypothesis, on a sample R01 did not use, with every instrument fixed before any data are retrieved.

What would fix it. Replace the sentence with an accurate timeline: R01 instruments frozen, then this frame harvested and graded for feasibility, then this protocol written from those numbers. That is a protocol after a pilot, not a confirmatory test with unseen data.

title: Review of P01v2: blocked
text:
Major findings

M1. Pinned code does not implement the stated locator rule. The extractor’s _text() retains visible text but discards xlink:
Reviewer chatgpt · Section 6.1 Extraction; 6.2 Grading
Pinned code does not implement the stated locator rule. The extractor’s _text() retains visible text but discards xlink:href targets. For PMC10202448, it retains ‘GitHub repository’ while losing the repository URL; REPO matches github.com rather than the bare repository name, producing ‘declarative’ under the pinned rules. Separately, grade_one(s) receives no article DOI or canonical URL, so it cannot exclude the article’s own identifiers. Its locator filter removes only an incomplete DOI-URL prefix, not matching article identifiers.

a named repository, or a DOI or URL that is not the article’s own

What would fix it. Preserve hyperlink targets and relevant data citations; pass normalized article identifiers into grading; distinguish article links from data/code locators. Verify these boundaries with real disclosures and negative examples before repinning.


M2. Query membership has no demonstrated validity as an instrument for research subject. The datashare query matches phrases
Reviewer chatgpt · Section 5. Exposure; 9. Threats, and what happened to each
Query membership has no demonstrated validity as an instrument for research subject. The datashare query matches phrases such as ‘code availability’ and ‘open data’ in titles, abstracts, and keywords without distinguishing an article studying sharing from one describing its own sharing. P6 validates meta-research eligibility, not this distinction. Outcome-related sharing language could therefore increase the probability of exposure classification, producing differential error and potentially inflating the association. Reproducibility of a query establishes neither construct validity nor bias toward the null.

it is reproducible from a query string, and its misclassification is toward the null.

What would fix it. Validate exposure against a blinded human assessment of research subject, including incidental mentions and descriptions of authors’ own sharing. Assess errors by outcome and arm. Alternatively, narrow the objective to association with query vocabulary and remove the asserted bias direction.


M3. P7 validates grading conditional on successful extraction, not ascertainment of the primary outcome. The supplied p7-gra
Reviewer chatgpt · Section 6.3 Validation of the grading rule; 10. The probes that must run before this is a protocol
P7 validates grading conditional on successful extraction, not ascertainment of the primary outcome. The supplied p7-grading-sample.csv contains 150 nonempty statements; the grading translation classifies 133 as declarative and 17 as actionable, with zero ‘none’ records. A person seeing only extracted text cannot discover omitted body statements or discarded hyperlink targets. Consequently, even perfect kappa could coexist with systematic, publisher-dependent false negatives in the analysis population.

150 statements, stratified by rule grade, are graded by the author, blind to the article’s exposure and to the rule’s grade.

What would fix it. Add an end-to-end validation sample of complete articles, including extraction negatives and each extraction route. Have humans independently identify and grade disclosures. Report actionable-outcome sensitivity and specificity by arm, alongside agreement, and make those results govern instrument acceptance.


M4. The proposed hand-graded co-primary analysis changes the population and estimand. P7 excludes every article without an e
Reviewer chatgpt · Section 6.3 Validation of the grading rule
The proposed hand-graded co-primary analysis changes the population and estimand. P7 excludes every article without an extracted statement, although those articles belong in the primary outcome’s negative category. It also samples by rule grade. An unweighted analysis of these records does not reproduce the association among all eligible articles. The actual file contains only 19 exposed articles and 17 rule-positive outcomes before eligibility screening, so it cannot inherit section 7’s power claims.

the primary analysis is repeated on the hand-graded subsample alone as a co-primary, with both reported together regardless of whether they agree.

What would fix it. Use a representative, adequately sized hand-assessed article sample that includes extraction negatives. If sampling is stratified, specify nonzero inclusion probabilities and an appropriate analysis. Define the co-primary decision rule and calculate its power separately.


M5. Fully open-access publication does not imply complete PMC deposition. NCBI distinguishes full participation, NIH-portfol
Reviewer chatgpt · Section 8. Analysis, sensitivity analysis 6; 9. Threats, and what happened to each
Fully open-access publication does not imply complete PMC deposition. NCBI distinguishes full participation, NIH-portfolio participation, and selective deposit; even full participation starts at a specified publication date. Thus the proposed restriction does not establish equal or complete ascertainment. See PMC participation agreements. Moreover, higher marginal PMC coverage in the exposed arm does not identify the direction of selection bias in the exposure-outcome association, contrary to section 9’s assertion that it favors the hypothesis.

Within a fully open-access journal every article is in PMC, so the differential selection that P2 exposed cannot operate.

What would fix it. Base this sensitivity on verified journal-year PMC coverage and usable XML availability, rather than open-access status alone. Remove the guarantee that selection cannot operate and the unsupported claim about its direction; state the restricted target population explicitly.


M6. Computed grid values do not establish the advertised power. probes.R solves an independent two-proportion normal approxi
Reviewer chatgpt · Section 7. Sample size and power
Computed grid values do not establish the advertised power. probes.R solves an independent two-proportion normal approximation, whereas the primary analysis estimates a journal-conditional odds ratio with year adjustment. It does not model journal clustering, exposure concentration, or screening losses separately by arm. Even its own approximation contradicts detection across OR 1.5–3: the worst cell requires OR 2.18, and OR 1.5 has approximately 30.5% power at baseline 0.038 and yield 0.5. Comparing R01’s 0.205 with this different frame’s 0.0384 also does not establish a lower bound on the screened baseline.

The design detects effects across that entire band

What would fix it. Calculate power for the planned mixed model using journal composition and separately justified screening yields for each arm. Include uncertainty in the screened baseline and validation fallbacks. Select a smallest effect of interest and report scenarios that fail to achieve its target power.


M7. A confidence interval containing 1 neither falsifies a positive association nor establishes absence. The same interval c
Reviewer chatgpt · Section 2. Objective and hypothesis; 7. Sample size and power
A confidence interval containing 1 neither falsifies a positive association nor establishes absence. The same interval can include substantial positive effects. Even a genuinely 80%-powered test fails to reject its null in about 20% of repetitions at the planning alternative. Power calculations do not turn nonsignificance into an equivalence test. The proposed rule could therefore label an inconclusive result as evidence against the hypothesis.

An adjusted odds ratio whose 95 percent confidence interval includes 1, in a sample powered as in section 7.

What would fix it. Prespecify a scientifically meaningful effect threshold and interpret the confidence interval against that threshold. Use an appropriate equivalence or effect-exclusion criterion for absence claims; classify sufficiently wide intervals as inconclusive.


M8. Outcome analysis has already occurred: P4 tabulates actionable outcomes by exposure, reporting 95/520 versus 132/3435, w
Reviewer chatgpt · Section Status callout; 1. Why this design exists; 7. Sample size and power; 8. Analysis
Outcome analysis has already occurred: P4 tabulates actionable outcomes by exposure, reporting 95/520 versus 132/3435, which reveals a crude odds ratio of approximately 5.59. Absence of a fitted regression does not make these outcomes unseen. Section 8 also calls analyses preregistered while the status says ‘Not registered’. The earlier e725b073034c4a777acbd1c10a375291be65e314 version already specified the primary model, so this is not evidence that the primary hypothesis was invented afterward; it is evidence that the account of prior outcome access is inaccurate.

No outcome has been analyzed under this protocol.

What would fix it. Provide an accurate timeline of specification, retrieval, arm-specific outcome summaries, and subsequent decisions. Distinguish pre-probe specifications from post-probe additions. Any decisions revised using these outcomes require an untouched evaluation sample for a prospective confirmatory claim, or explicit exploratory labeling.


M9. The claimed executable analysis does not implement P01v2. The pinned R01 analyze.R hardcodes R01 input paths, derives ex
Reviewer chatgpt · Section 13. Availability; 8. Analysis
The claimed executable analysis does not implement P01v2. The pinned R01 analyze.R hardcodes R01 input paths, derives exposure from topic_datashare rather than the new frame’s arm definition, retains article-type adjustment, and lacks P01v2 screening/validation branches and sensitivities 3, 5, and 6. The confirmatory directory contains probe code, not an analysis driver implementing the stated protocol. Running the identified analysis unchanged would analyze the wrong sample under the wrong specification.

The analysis code that will run is already written and public; it is the code that produced R01, and section 6 pins it.

What would fix it. Provide and pin a P01v2 analysis driver implementing the declared sample, exposure, validation contingencies, primary and secondary models, and all six sensitivities. Include reproducible sample-generation procedures and a documented command that consumes the confirmatory inputs.


M10. The protocol says a 95 percent CI that includes 1, in a sample powered as in section 7, can be read as evidence of absen
Reviewer grok · Section 2. Objective and hypothesis
The protocol says a 95 percent CI that includes 1, in a sample powered as in section 7, can be read as evidence of absence. Power to detect an odds ratio of 2.18 at 80 percent is not power to rule out 1.5, and it is not an equivalence test. There is no smallest effect size of interest and no TOST or CI-exclusion rule against a margin. Failure to reject OR=1 remains absence of evidence for anything smaller than the detectable value. The mixed model in section 8 is also less powered than the two-proportion calculation used in section 7, because data-availability statements cluster by journal.

Section 7 fixes the power in advance so that a null can be read as evidence of absence rather than absence of evidence, which was not true of R01.

What would fix it. State a smallest odds ratio that would still matter (for example 1.5). Falsify only if the 95 percent CI lies entirely below that margin, or run a preregistered equivalence test. Recompute power for glmer with (1|journal) under a plausible ICC. Delete the claim that a null here is evidence of absence.


M11. Three power claims do not survive the protocol’s own numbers and files. First, section 2 says 1.5 to 3 would be consiste
Reviewer grok · Section 7. Sample size and power
Three power claims do not survive the protocol’s own numbers and files. First, section 2 says 1.5 to 3 would be consistent with R01 and section 7 says the design detects that entire band. On the protocol’s own grid, at yield 0.5 and baseline 0.038 the detectable OR is 2.18, so 1.5 is not detectable in the cell treated as worst case. Second, the grid never goes below yield 0.5, but the unlabeled P6 title list is not a 50 percent meta-research sample. The comparison titles are mostly clinical systematic reviews and meta-analyses of patient outcomes (the report block’s PRISMA/CONSORT phrases and the qualifier ‘we searched PubMed’ retrieve ordinary reviews). The exposed titles include database papers, resource descriptions, and clinical studies that mention data sharing (Scientific Data alone is 17 exposed and 1 comparison in the full-text frame). A yield of 0.15 at baseline 0.038 gives a detectable OR of about 3.49, which trips the protocol’s own P5 rule that a detectable effect above about 2.5 means the frame must be widened. Third, the unscreened 18.3 percent vs 3.8 percent contrast is not a lower bound on the screened contrast: screening should remove data journals from the exposed arm (lowering the exposed rate) as well as clinical reviews from the comparison arm (raising the comparison rate). The power calculation never allows those rates to move in opposite directions.

The design detects effects across that entire band, which is the property R01 lacked: its floor was roughly 3.7, so it could only ever have seen an effect as large as the one it reported.

What would fix it. Treat the P6 file as a yield probe before claiming power. Estimate yield (and yield by arm) from the 200 titles, or from a hand-screened subset, and rebuild the grid down to that yield. If the worst-case detectable OR exceeds 2.5, widen the frame or drop the claims that the design detects 1.5 and that a null rules something out. Separate the unscreened mixture rates from the screened target population.


M12. Section 9 asserts that differential PMC coverage favors the hypothesis. Section 12 says the direction of bias on the bet
Reviewer grok · Section 9. Threats, and what happened to each
Section 9 asserts that differential PMC coverage favors the hypothesis. Section 12 says the direction of bias on the between-arm comparison is not obvious and is not claimed toward the null. Both cannot stand. If section 9 is right, the primary glmer on the PMC full-text set is biased in the direction of a positive finding, and the analysis that was added to block that path is only sensitivity 6. If section 12 is right, section 9’s directional claim should be withdrawn. The 20-point PMC gap is large enough that this is not a side issue.

Arms are differentially selected into the analysis set and the direction favors the hypothesis.

What would fix it. Pick one account of the bias and make the analysis that removes differential PMC selection the primary (for example, journals in which every sampled article is in PMC, with that rule defined before seeing outcomes). Keep the current model as a sensitivity. Align sections 9 and 12.


M13. Section 12 calls the qualified frame a high-precision slice. The qualifier includes ‘we searched PubMed’, ‘publications’
Reviewer grok · Section 12. What this design still cannot do
Section 12 calls the qualified frame a high-precision slice. The qualifier includes ‘we searched PubMed’, ‘publications’, and ‘PRISMA statement’ via the report block, which is how ordinary clinical reviews enter. That is a precision failure, not only the recall failure section 12 describes (papers that say ‘we examined 300 trials’ drop out). The P6 titles are the evidence. High precision is the claim that screening was supposed to earn, not a property of the harvested frame.

The sample is a high-precision slice of the field, not the field.

What would fix it. Describe the qualified frame as high-recall for papers that mention literature-search boilerplate and low-precision for meta-research. Put the precision claim only after screening, and only if P6 kappa and yield support it.


M14. The written rule grades a DOI or URL as actionable only when it is not the article’s own DOI. grade_one() takes only the
Reviewer grok · Section 6.2 Grading
The written rule grades a DOI or URL as actionable only when it is not the article’s own DOI. grade_one() takes only the statement string. It never receives the article DOI. The filter loc[!str_detect(loc, ‘doi.org/10.[0-9]{4,9}/$’)] drops only a DOI URL with an empty path, not this article’s DOI and not the journal site. The comment in grade.R claims the journal site is excluded; that is not implemented either. On the confirmatory frame, 38 of 227 actionable grades are URL/DOI without a named repository (12 exposed, 26 comparison). Those are exactly the grades this clause is supposed to police.

A DOI or URL present that is not the article’s own DOI: actionable.

What would fix it. Pass each article’s DOI (and host) into the grader and drop locators that match them, or change test 4 to match the code. Pin the revised function and re-run P4/P7.


M15. The screening instrument is not pinned. Extract.py is pinned to a commit hash; screening is ’two models from different p
Reviewer grok · Section 4.3 Screening
The screening instrument is not pinned. Extract.py is pinned to a commit hash; screening is ‘two models from different providers’ with no model identifiers, no prompt, no temperature, and no code path. Later in section 10 the protocol allows P6 to use a single model while a reviewer is quota-blocked. Dual-review screening then cannot run, and single-model screening is not one of the stated fallbacks (the stated fallback is author screening of a subsample). The author is also not blind to exposure or to the P4 association when adjudicating disagreements.

Screening is on title and abstract, by two models from different providers, each given the same written criterion and blind to the other.

What would fix it. Pin model names, the full screening prompt, and decoding settings in the repository at a commit hash, as was done for extract.py. If only one model is available, use the written fallback (author-screened subsample, power recomputed) rather than an unlisted single-model screen. Keep the author’s adjudication blind to arm and to P4 rates.


M16. P7 is described as 150 statements stratified by rule grade. The file studies/P01v2-confirmatory/out/p7-grading-sample.cs
Reviewer grok · Section 6.3 Validation of the grading rule
P7 is described as 150 statements stratified by rule grade. The file studies/P01v2-confirmatory/out/p7-grading-sample.csv has 150 non-empty statements, 0 empties, and under the pinned rule 17 actionable and 133 declarative. Equal stratification on three grades would be about 50 each, including none. Equal stratification on the two non-none grades would be about 75/75. 17/133 matches a simple random sample of extracted statements (frame: 227 actionable of 1688 statements, 13.4 percent; P7: 11.3 percent). The most common analysis grade, none, is unvalidated. Kappa on 17 actionable items is a noisy gate for the 0.80 / 0.60 thresholds. No script in the repository produces this file, so the sampling is not itself pinned.

150 statements, stratified by rule grade, are graded by the author, blind to the article’s exposure and to the rule’s grade.

What would fix it. Draw 50 none, 50 declarative, and 50 actionable, or draw a prevalence-weighted sample and say so. Put the sampler in the repo. Report kappa for the primary binary (actionable vs not) on a sample that includes none. Do not treat agreement on boilerplate declarative statements as agreement on the primary outcome.


M17. Sensitivity 3 restricts to journals with at least 10 articles in each arm. In the full-text frame that is 4 journals (BM
Reviewer grok · Section 8. Analysis
Sensitivity 3 restricts to journals with at least 10 articles in each arm. In the full-text frame that is 4 journals (BMJ Open, PLOS ONE, Journal of medical Internet research, F1000Research). Scientific Data, the journal that most confounds exposure with policy (17 exposed, 1 comparison), is dropped. That is not a general within-journal estimate. Sensitivity 6 is the analysis meant to block differential PMC selection, but ‘fully open-access journal’ is undefined, and the supporting sentence is false: gold OA is not the same as PMC deposit, and PMC also holds author manuscripts from non-OA journals. OpenAlex oa_status is already in data/lit/openalex-frame-P01v2-summary.json and is not used. The multiplicity paragraph says five sensitivities; there are six. There is no P01v2 analyze.R; year_c is not defined here (R01 used year minus 2020); sensitivity 4 says authorship but R01 used a repository-name regex in the statement.

Within a fully open-access journal every article is in PMC, so the differential selection that P2 exposed cannot operate.

What would fix it. Probe how many journals pass the 10-per-arm rule and either drop sensitivity 3 or replace it with all journals that published both arms. Define sensitivity 6 with an operational OA/PMC rule (for example, journals whose articles in this frame are 100 percent PMC, or OpenAlex gold+diamond) and do not equate OA with PMC. Write the analysis script this protocol actually specifies. Count six sensitivities.


M18. P3’s stated design-change rule is a route distribution unlike tier A’s. R01 title-matching routes were about 16 percent
Reviewer grok · Section 10. The probes that must run before this is a protocol
P3’s stated design-change rule is a route distribution unlike tier A’s. R01 title-matching routes were about 16 percent of the exposed arm and 7 percent of the comparison arm. On this frame, among full-text records, title-matching routes are 5.0 percent exposed (26/520) and 9.3 percent comparison (318/3435): the imbalance reversed. The protocol never reports that comparison and does not say why it does not change the design. P4’s stated output is the comparison-arm grade distribution; the probe and section 7 both emit the exposed arm as well.

A route distribution unlike tier A’s means publishers differ between frames and journal adjustment is carrying more weight than assumed

What would fix it. Report the P3 route table against R01, and either justify keeping the design or add the journal-weight consequence P3 said would follow. Describe P4 as what it actually computed: both arms.


M19. Section 13 says the analysis code that will run is already written and is the code that produced R01. studies/P01-advoca
Reviewer grok · Section 13. Availability
Section 13 says the analysis code that will run is already written and is the code that produced R01. studies/P01-advocacy-and-practice/R/analyze.R fits art_type, does not exclude comments/editorials up front, does not implement sensitivities 3, 5, or 6, and flags the author’s papers by matching ‘choxos|sofi-mahmudi’ in the statement rather than by authorship. There is no analyze.R under studies/P01v2-confirmatory/. The primary model in section 8 is a different model.

The analysis code that will run is already written and public; it is the code that produced R01, and section 6 pins it.

What would fix it. Write and pin the analysis script that implements section 8, including the six sensitivities and an operational rule for the author’s papers. Do not point at R01’s analyzer as the code that will run.

title: Do trials quietly cut their enrollment target?
text:
The question
A trial registration carries a planned enrollment that can be revised. A trial that starts, struggles to recruit, and lowers its target has not failed in any registry field: the final record shows the new target as if it had always been the plan. Whether trials that revise downward after starting are less likely to post results, and whether they report their shortfall when they do, needs the history of the record, not its current state.

1. The question
A trial registration asks whether individual participant data will be shared. The answer is a pledge made before anyone knows what the trial will find. Results posting is a later, observable act of openness. Whether trials that pledged openness then behave openly, or whether the pledge is costless signaling, is a test of stated against revealed transparency on a very large sample.

title: Does meta-research do parachute research?
text:
1. The question
Parachute research, in which investigators from wealthy countries study populations elsewhere without local collaborators, is criticized in global health. Meta-research has its own version: studies that grade the transparency, reporting or integrity of research from a named country. Whether such studies include anyone from the country whose research they are grading, and whether that depends on the country’s income, has not been asked of the field that asks it of everyone else.

title: Do null results stay preprints?
text:
1. The question
Publication bias is usually measured as studies that never appear. Preprints make a new measurement possible: a study that did appear, publicly, and then did or did not make it into a journal. If null results reach journals less often or more slowly, the preprint server is holding part of the file drawer in public, and the journal literature is biased by exactly the mechanism meta-research documents in trials.

title: Does rtransparency see what a person sees in meta-research articles?
text:
ImportantStatus: design. No probe has run.



Written against the design standard.
Disclosure. The author maintains rtransparency and would code the reference standard. A tool’s maintainer validating the tool is a conflict. The mitigation is blind coding, a second coder on a subset, and publication of every disagreement. It is stated here because it cannot be removed.

title: Does rtransparency see what a person sees in meta-research articles?
text:
1. The question
P13, P14, P23 and P27 in this program, and any successor to P01v2, use rtransparency as their instrument. Its published accuracy comes from a benchmark of the general biomedical literature: for data sharing, sensitivity 0.765 and specificity 0.990 (rt_accuracy). Whether those numbers hold on meta-research articles, which is the literature most of these studies read, is unmeasured. A detector can transport badly: meta-research authors may write data statements in a more conventional form, and their articles discuss data sharing as a topic, which a detector can mistake for the article’s own statement. The second of those is the artifact that contaminated R01.
This design is infrastructure. Every study that uses the instrument needs its answer.

title: Does rtransparency see what a person sees in meta-research articles?
section: 2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim
text:
2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim
Log key P22.
corpus regex: (rtransparent|rtransparency|automated (detection|assessment)|text.mining)
              .{0,80}(transparen|data sharing|indicator).{0,80}(valid|accura|sensitiv)
PubMed:       (rtransparent[tiab] OR rtransparency[tiab] OR ODDPub[tiab]
              OR "automated detection"[tiab] OR "text mining"[tiab]
              OR "natural language processing"[tiab]) AND ("data sharing"[tiab]
              OR "transparency indicators"[tiab] OR "open data"[tiab])
              AND (validation[tiab] OR accuracy[tiab] OR sensitivity[tiab])
Thirty-six PubMed records. The relevant ones apply transparency indicators to other literatures: infectious disease models (PMID 36206207), space medicine (PMID 38564591), infectious disease journals (PMID 37132475). The original validation is Serghiou and colleagues 2021, PLOS Biology, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.3001107, taken from the package’s own citation record rather than from memory. The search found no validation on meta-research articles.

title: Does rtransparency see what a person sees in meta-research articles?
text:
3. Hypothesis
On meta-research articles, rtransparency’s specificity for data sharing is lower than its published 0.990, because these articles discuss data sharing as their subject.
Null. Specificity on meta-research articles equals 0.990.
What would falsify it. Specificity whose interval includes 0.990. The detector would then transport without this failure, and the studies that depend on it could say so.
Sensitivity, and the accuracy of the other six detectors, are estimated and reported without a directional hypothesis.

title: Does rtransparency see what a person sees in meta-research articles?
text:
4. Design and unit
Diagnostic accuracy study against a reference standard. One article is one unit.

title: Does rtransparency see what a person sees in meta-research articles?
text:
5. Sample
Tier A articles with PMC full text. A stratified random sample of 300, stratified on the detector’s own prediction for data sharing so that both sensitivity and specificity are estimated with useful precision; stratum weights are the inverse sampling fractions. Articles whose subject is data sharing, by the datashare label, are oversampled within strata, because they are where the hypothesized failure lives. This P22 sample must not overlap any study’s analysis sample, and the sampled PMCIDs are published so later studies can exclude them.

title: Does rtransparency see what a person sees in meta-research articles?
text:
6. Reference standard
The author codes each article for the seven indicators against the definitions in Serghiou 2021, without seeing the detector’s output, from the full text as a reader would see it. A written rubric specifies, among other things, that an article’s discussion of other articles’ data sharing is not its own data sharing statement.
A second coder independently codes 60 of the 300. Inter-coder kappa is reported per indicator.

text:
7. Analysis
In R. Weighted sensitivity and specificity per indicator, with the sampling weights, and bootstrap confidence intervals resampling within strata. Estimates are reported beside rt_accuracy’s published values.
Preregistered alongside: accuracy separately for articles with and without the datashare label, and a list of every disagreement between detector and reference, with the text that caused it.

title: Do papers that read like a language model cite references that do not exist?
text:
1. The question
Language models invent references, and that is documented for chatbot output. Whether invented references have reached the published literature, and whether they concentrate in articles whose prose shows the vocabulary that language models overuse, is a different question. It asks about what has been published, not what a chatbot produces when asked.

section: 2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim

2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim

corpus regex: (hallucinat|fabricat|fake|nonexistent|non-existent).{0,40}(reference|citation)

              OR "non-existent"[tiab] OR fake[tiab]) AND (reference*[tiab] OR citation*[tiab])
              AND ("large language model*"[tiab] OR ChatGPT[tiab] OR "generative AI"[tiab])
One hundred and seventy-six PubMed records. The relevant ones measure fabricated references in chatbot output: for systematic review queries (PMID 38776130) and for medical content (PMID 37337480). The relevance-ordered top ten contains no study relating vocabulary in published articles to reference validity.

title: Do papers that read like a language model cite references that do not exist?
text:
3. Hypothesis
In articles published from 2023, a higher vocabulary-excess score is associated with a larger share of references that cannot be resolved; in articles published before 2023 it is not.
Null. The interaction between vocabulary excess and period is 0.
What would falsify it. No interaction: an association of the same size before 2023 would mean the score measures something other than model use, such as field or writing style, and the pre-2023 period is included precisely as that negative control.

title: Do papers that read like a language model cite references that do not exist?
text:
4. Design and unit
Cross-sectional with a pre-period negative control. One article is one unit.

title: Do papers that read like a language model cite references that do not exist?
text:
5. Sample
PMC open-access research articles from 2019 to 2025, sampled evenly by year. A development slice of 10 percent, drawn first and never analyzed, is used only to build the vocabulary score (S1).

title: Do papers that read like a language model cite references that do not exist?
text:
6. Exposure
Vocabulary-excess score. On the development slice, the words whose frequency per million tokens in 2024 exceeds their 2021 frequency by a ratio fixed in advance form the marker list. The score for an article is the marker frequency in its body. Built once, frozen, and published with the protocol before the analysis slice is touched.

title: Do papers that read like a language model cite references that do not exist?
text:
7. Outcome and instrument
The proportion of an article’s references that cannot be resolved. A reference with a DOI in pub-id[@pub-id-type='doi'] is resolved against Crossref. A reference without one is matched on title against Crossref and OpenAlex with a similarity threshold. Unresolved references are further split into malformed DOIs, well-formed DOIs that resolve to nothing, and titles with no match.
The denominator is references the method can attempt. Book chapters, reports and web pages are counted and excluded, since failing to match a report is not evidence it does not exist.

title: Do papers that read like a language model cite references that do not exist?
text:
8. Validation gate
The author checks 200 unresolved references by hand against library catalogues and search engines, coding each as real, garbled real, or nonexistent. The primary outcome is recomputed as the proportion coded nonexistent; if fewer than 20 percent of unresolved references are nonexistent, unresolvability measures metadata quality rather than invention and the hypothesis is tested on the hand-checked subset only.

In R.
glmmTMB(cbind(unresolved, attempted - unresolved) ~ score * post2023 + (1 | journal),
        family = betabinomial, data = d)
Preregistered alongside: the same model using the hand-coded nonexistent share on the validation subset, and a model excluding journals with fewer than 20 sampled articles.

text:
1. The question
An ORCID identifier that a publisher has authenticated ties a byline to a person who logged in to claim it. A paper mill selling authorship slots, or inventing authors, has less reason to produce that link. The share of a paper’s authors carrying an authenticated ORCID is therefore a candidate integrity signal that is cheap to compute for every article ever published.

corpus regex: ORCID.{0,80}(retract|misconduct|integrity|paper mill)
PubMed:       ORCID[tiab] AND (retract*[tiab] OR "paper mill*"[tiab]
              OR misconduct[tiab] OR "research integrity"[tiab])
Seven PubMed records, none in the corpus. The closest proposes recording retractions on ORCID profiles (PMID 38815635); another discusses author name ambiguity (PMID 38704656). None measures ORCID coverage as a marker of retraction risk.

title: Do misconduct retractions have fewer verified authors?
text:
3. Hypothesis
Articles retracted for misconduct-class reasons have a smaller share of authors with an authenticated ORCID than matched controls; articles retracted for honest error do not.

What would falsify it. No association for misconduct, or an equal association for honest error, which would point to journal-level practice rather than to fraud.

title: Do misconduct retractions have fewer verified authors?
text:

Cases and reason classes as defined in P17, from Retraction Watch with a DOI, published 2016 or later, when publisher ORCID deposit to Crossref became common. Controls: four per case, same journal and publication month, not in Retraction Watch (S9).

title: Do misconduct retractions have fewer verified authors?
text:
6. Exposure
The share of an article’s authors whose Crossref author record carries an ORCID with authenticated-orcid true. OpenAlex attaches ORCIDs by inference as well as from publisher deposit, and an inferred ORCID says nothing about whether the author claimed the paper, so OpenAlex is used only for a sensitivity analysis and never for the primary exposure (S3).

Case or control status, by reason class.

text:

The reason mapping is validated in P17. Here, the author checks for 100 articles that the Crossref record’s authenticated ORCIDs match the ORCIDs printed on the publisher page. Below 95 percent agreement, the exposure is recomputed from the source that agrees with the article.

clogit(case ~ I(auth_share * 10) + log(n_authors) + strata(match_set), data = d)

title: Do senior authors get listed for reviewing rather than doing?
text:
1. The question
Honorary authorship has been studied mostly by asking authors. The CRediT taxonomy now records, in machine-readable form, what each author says they did. An author whose only declared role is “Writing: review and editing” appears on the byline without a declared hand in the work. Whether that pattern concentrates among senior authors is a direct, behavioral test of the gift authorship hypothesis, using the authors’ own declarations.

title: Do senior authors get listed for reviewing rather than doing?
section: 2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim
text:
2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim
Log key P16.
corpus regex: CRediT|contributor roles? taxonomy
PubMed:       ("CRediT"[tiab] OR "contributor roles taxonomy"[tiab]
              OR "contributor role taxonomy"[tiab]) AND (authorship[tiab]
              OR "gift authorship"[tiab] OR "honorary authorship"[tiab] OR seniority[tiab])
Two hundred and eighty PubMed records, twenty-six in the corpus. The relevance-ordered top ten are about authorship and credit in general, such as the gendered nature of authorship (PMID 34516891), shared first authorship (PMID 31607826) and authorship and contributorship (PMID 24644440). None in the top ten relates declared roles to author seniority. This is the weakest novelty claim of this set and says so: the space is large and the top ten is not the whole of it. Probe PD widens the search before any data are retrieved.

title: Do senior authors get listed for reviewing rather than doing?
text:
3. Hypothesis
The probability that an author’s declared roles contain no substantive contribution rises with the author’s seniority, conditional on author position and team size.
Null. The coefficient on seniority is 0.
What would falsify it. A coefficient at or below 0.

text:
4. Design and unit
Cross-sectional, author-level. One author on one article is one unit; articles and authors both recur, and the model treats them as crossed.

title: Do senior authors get listed for reviewing rather than doing?
text:
5. Sample
PMC open-access research articles, 2020 to 2025, whose JATS carries role elements with the CRediT vocabulary for every listed author. Articles where only some authors have roles are excluded and counted, because a missing role cannot be read as no contribution.

title: Do senior authors get listed for reviewing rather than doing?
text:
6. Exposure
Seniority at the article’s publication date: years since the author’s first indexed publication in OpenAlex. OpenAlex author disambiguation merges and splits people; section 10 carries this.

title: Do senior authors get listed for reviewing rather than doing?
text:
7. Outcome
Minimal role set: every declared role is in {Writing: review and editing, Funding acquisition, Resources}. Every other CRediT role, including Supervision, counts as substantive. Counting Supervision as substantive works against the hypothesis, because supervision is a legitimately senior role; the choice is made so that a positive result cannot be produced by it.
Roles are read from JATS role elements and their vocab-term attributes, not from free-text contribution statements (S2).

glmer(minimal ~ ns(seniority_years, 3) + position + log(team_size)

Position is first, last, or middle. Preregistered alongside: the same model restricted to middle authors, where position carries least information, and a sensitivity analysis dropping authors whose OpenAlex record implies a career longer than 50 years at the article date, which marks records that probably merge more than one person.

ImportantStatus: design. No probe has run.

title: Did the NIH data sharing policy change what papers share?
text:
1. The question
The NIH Data Management and Sharing Policy took effect on 25 January 2023 and applies to competing applications received from that date. It is the largest funder mandate for data sharing in biomedicine. Whether papers from covered awards share data more than papers from uncovered awards published at the same time is an empirical question the policy’s own documentation cannot answer.
The policy creates a comparison that is rare in this field: in any given month, papers are being published both from awards the policy covers and from older awards it does not.

title: Did the NIH data sharing policy change what papers share?
section: 2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim
text:
2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim
Log key P14.
corpus regex: (NIH|National Institutes of Health).{0,60}
              (data management and sharing|DMS policy|data sharing policy)
PubMed:       ("data management and sharing policy"[tiab] OR "DMS policy"[tiab]
              OR ("NIH"[tiab] AND "data sharing policy"[tiab]))
Forty-two PubMed records. The relevant ones describe or advise on the policy: a commentary on open data and the 2023 policy (PMID 36862609), one on building on it (PMID 38753788), rules for writing a sharing plan (PMID 35921268), and an evaluation of sharing-plan templates (PMID 41445711). The search found none that measures sharing in the resulting publications against a concurrent control.

title: Did the NIH data sharing policy change what papers share?
text:
3. Hypothesis
Articles from awards covered by the policy carry a data sharing statement that rtransparency detects as open data more often than articles from uncovered awards published in the same month.
Null. The odds ratio, covered against uncovered, adjusted for month, is 1.
What would falsify it. An odds ratio at or below 1: the mandate produced plans without producing shared data in papers. That result would matter more than the positive one.

title: Did the NIH data sharing policy change what papers share?
text:
4. Design and unit
Concurrent-control comparison with month fixed effects, and an event-time analysis by months since award. One article linked to one award is one unit; the award is the cluster.

title: Did the NIH data sharing policy change what papers share?
text:
5. Sample
PMC open-access articles published from February 2023 to the latest complete month, each linked to an NIH award through the RePORTER publications endpoint. Covered: the linked award is a new or competing renewal application received on or after 2023-01-25. Uncovered: the linked award’s latest competing application predates the policy. An article linked to awards of both kinds is excluded and counted, since its exposure is not defined.

title: Did the NIH data sharing policy change what papers share?
text:
6. Exposure
Policy coverage of the linked award, from RePORTER application type and dates.

title: Did the NIH data sharing policy change what papers share?
text:
7. Outcome and instrument
rtransparency::rt_data_code_pmc on the PMC XML, is_open_data as primary and is_open_code as secondary. Published accuracy for open data: sensitivity 0.765, specificity 0.990 (rt_accuracy).
The threat that matters most is differential misclassification. The detector was built on statements written before the policy. If covered awards produce statements in a new style, such as a pointer to a sharing plan or to a controlled-access repository, sensitivity may differ by arm, and a difference in detected sharing could be a difference in detection.

title: Did the NIH data sharing policy change what papers share?
text:
8. Validation gate
The author codes 200 articles, 100 per arm, blind to arm and to detector output, against the rtransparent definitions. Sensitivity is estimated per arm. If it differs by more than 0.10, the uncorrected odds ratio is not reported and only the arm-corrected estimate is (S3).

In R.
glmer(open_data ~ covered + factor(pub_month) + (1 | award) + (1 | journal),
      family = binomial, data = d)
Preregistered alongside: an event-time model on months from award start to publication, and a probabilistic bias analysis using the arm-specific accuracies. Power is simulated for this model at the realized counts before it is fitted (S12).

text:
ImportantStatus: design. No probe has run.

title: Are old prevalence estimates cited as if they were current?
text:
1. The question
“Only 12 percent of trials share their data” is a sentence that can be true in the year it was measured and misleading ten years later. Meta-research produces prevalence estimates that other papers then quote. Whether the quotation carries the estimate’s date, or presents an old number as the current state of the world, has not been measured.

title: Are old prevalence estimates cited as if they were current?
section: 2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim
text:
2. Prior work, and the search behind the novelty claim
Log key P12.
corpus regex: (outdated|stale|obsolete).{0,40}(citation|cited|evidence)
              |citation.{0,30}(accuracy|context).{0,40}(prevalence|estimate)
PubMed:       ("citation accuracy"[tiab] OR "quotation accuracy"[tiab]
              OR "citation context"[tiab] OR "outdated evidence"[tiab])
              AND (prevalence[tiab] OR estimate*[tiab])
Ten PubMed records, none in the corpus. Quotation accuracy is established territory: a systematic review and meta-analysis of quotation accuracy in medical journals (PMID 26528420), a review of methods for checking cited facts (PMID 28910404), and a study of citation inaccuracies in surgical literature (PMID 35130090). Those ask whether a citation misstates what the source says. This asks something they do not: whether a correctly quoted number is presented as current when it is not.

title: Are old prevalence estimates cited as if they were current?
text:
3. Hypothesis
Citation sentences written by meta-research authors date the estimate they cite more often than citation sentences written by other authors, adjusted for the estimate’s age.
Null. The odds ratio for dated framing, meta-research citers against other citers, is 1.
What would falsify it. An odds ratio at or below 1: the field that produces the estimates is no more careful about their age than anyone else.
The descriptive quantity reported alongside, but not tested, is the proportion of citations presenting an estimate more than ten years old in the present tense.

title: Are old prevalence estimates cited as if they were current?
text:
4. Design and unit
Cross-sectional study of citation sentences. One citation sentence is one unit; the citing article is the cluster.

title: Are old prevalence estimates cited as if they were current?
text:
5. Sample
Cited set: tier A articles whose abstract reports a prevalence of a research practice (a proportion of articles, trials or reviews with a property). Identified by a classifier gated on the author’s labels, because a regex for “percent of” retrieves results of every kind.
Citing set: PMC open-access articles that cite a member of the cited set, from OpenAlex, one citation sentence per citing-cited pair. Where an article cites the same estimate twice, the first mention is used.

title: Are old prevalence estimates cited as if they were current?
text:
6. Exposure
Whether the citing article is itself meta-research, by the tier A vocabulary match on the citing article. This is a label, not a judgment, and misclassification here is toward the null.

title: Are old prevalence estimates cited as if they were current?
text:
7. Outcome and instrument
Dated framing: the sentence gives the estimate’s year, its study period, or an explicit temporal qualifier (“in 2014”, “at the time”, “an earlier study found”). Current framing: present tense with no temporal qualifier. Mixed or unclear sentences are a third class, analyzed separately.
The citation sentence is located through the JATS xref pointing at the reference, not by searching text for an author name (S2).

title: Are old prevalence estimates cited as if they were current?
text:
8. Validation gate
The author labels 250 citation sentences against a written rubric with examples of each class. A model classifies them blind. Kappa is computed on the dated-versus-current contrast that enters the model; below 0.75 the study stops at the author-labeled sample and is reported as a descriptive study of that sample.

text:
9. Analysis
In R.
glmer(dated ~ citer_is_metaresearch + ns(estimate_age, 3) + (1 | citing_article)
      + (1 | cited_article), family = binomial, data = d)
Crossed random effects, because both citing and cited articles recur. Estimate age is the years between the cited study’s data collection end, or its publication if that is not stated, and the citing article’s publication date.

title: Does meta-research have a file drawer?

1. The question
Meta-research measures non-publication in other fields and treats it as waste. It publishes its own protocols in journals such as BMJ Open and Systematic Reviews, and nobody has checked how many of those protocols are followed by the study they describe. If the field’s own protocols go unpublished at a high rate, it has the file drawer it documents elsewhere.

3. Hypothesis
A meta-research protocol published in a journal is followed by a results paper within 36 months less often than a trial protocol published in the same journal in the same year.
Null. The hazard ratio for results publication, meta-research against trial protocols, is 1.
What would falsify it. A hazard ratio at or above 1. Meta-research has no regulatory obligation to publish and much of it is student work, which is the reasoning behind the direction. The reverse finding would be as publishable.

title: Does meta-research have a file drawer?
text:
4. Design and unit

title: Does meta-research have a file drawer?
text:
5. Sample

Comparison: trial protocols (title contains “protocol” and publication type or abstract names a randomized trial) from the same journal and publication year, sampled 2 to 1 without replacement (S9). A journal-year with fewer than two trial protocols contributes all it has and is weighted accordingly; a journal-year with none drops its exposed protocols, and the count is reported.

If sensitivity differs between arms by more than 0.10, the study reports arm-specific corrected estimates and does not report an uncorrected hazard ratio.

The author scores a random sample of 150 articles. Precise, and the ceiling on sample size.

title: Do meta-research conclusions soften between preprint and journal?
text:
ImportantStatus: reduced protocol, by the decision rule this document wrote before the number was known.



Both linkage probes have run. 66 of 1790 tier A records and 75 of 7572 frame records have a preprint version: 141 pairs, a rate of 3.7 and 1.0 percent respectively.
Section 4 stated, before either number was known, that 200 or more pairs makes this a full protocol, 80 to 200 makes it a reduced one with a single binary outcome and no subgroup analyses, and under 80 makes it an agenda item. 141 falls in the middle band, so the reduced form is what this document now specifies. The rule is applied as written rather than renegotiated, which is the only thing that made writing it in advance worth doing.
Restricting to biomedical preprint servers, excluding arXiv and SSRN, leaves 108 pairs, which is still inside the 80 to 200 band. The biomedical restriction is therefore the primary analysis, not a subgroup, because this project is about biomedical meta-research and a result carried by arXiv preprints would not be about that.
A first draft of this section asserted that 108 was “below the 80 the rule requires” and used that to justify keeping arXiv in the primary analysis. 108 is not below 80. The claim contradicted the number printed two sentences above it, and it is recorded here rather than silently corrected because it is the third time in this project that a sentence reasoning about a computed value came out backwards.

title: Do meta-research conclusions soften between preprint and journal?
text:
1. The question
Meta-research criticizes the literature, and peer reviewers are drawn from the literature being criticized. If review systematically blunts that criticism, the published record understates what the field found, and the preprint is the only place the original claim survives.
This is measurable because meta-research increasingly appears as a preprint first, and both versions persist.

title: The field is observational about itself
section: Why this matters rather than merely being true
text:
Why this matters rather than merely being true
Meta-research grades other fields on their evidence hierarchy. It tells clinical researchers that an observational association is weaker than a randomized comparison, and it is right. Its own output is almost entirely observational association.
Some of that is unavoidable. You cannot randomize whether a paper was preregistered. But the questions the field most wants answered are causal and several of them are randomizable: whether a reporting checklist at submission improves reporting, whether blinding reviewers changes what gets accepted, whether a data availability mandate produces available data or only statements. Each of those is an intervention on a process someone controls.

title: The field is observational about itself
section: Why it cannot be run here
text:
Why it cannot be run here
Every such experiment requires randomizing something inside a journal, a funder or an ethics committee: which manuscripts get an intervention, which reviewers see what, which applicants receive which instruction. None of that is reachable from public data, and no amount of harvesting substitutes for the permission.
The honest statement is that this project can measure the gap and cannot fill it. Recording that is more useful than inventing an observational proxy and calling it an answer, which is precisely the substitution the field is criticized for elsewhere.

title: The field is observational about itself
text:
What would make it runnable
A partner willing to randomize one thing: a journal, a preprint server, a funder, or a conference with a submission process. The design is not the obstacle and would be short. The access is the obstacle.

title: The field is observational about itself
section: The one caveat on the measurement
text:
The one caveat on the measurement
Publication type is assigned by NLM indexing and an experiment can be missed. 515 of the corpus records carry no MeSH indexing at all, mostly the most recent, and an unindexed experiment would not appear in the count above. The number is a floor, not a point estimate, and the floor is four.

ImportantStatus: BLOCKED BY REVIEW on 2026-09-19. Do not run this.

The most concrete finding is verified and correct. The temporal classification is wrong. probes.py compares calendar years, so every same-year match falls into pre-retraction by default. Recounting: 83 strictly post, 66 strictly pre, and 41 same-year that the probe reported as pre-retraction and which are actually undetermined. The reviewers also found, independently of each other, that the comparison arm does not exist: the document promises articles matched on journal and year, and what it actually specifies is whatever screening excludes, with no matching ratio, no replacement rule and no weighting. And that section 7’s feasibility numbers were computed over both caches without applying this study’s own eligibility criteria, so they describe a different population from the one the protocol defines.
Left exactly as submitted. A successor will be a new document.

title: Does meta-research cite retracted work?
text:
1. The question
Citing a retracted paper as though it still stands is a documented failure of the literature, and meta-research is the field that documents it. Retracted randomized trials have been shown to go on being cited uncorrected in systematic reviews and clinical guidelines (PMID 35779825), and guidelines for low back pain have been shown to cite retracted and predatory work (PMID 40156953).
Nobody has turned that instrument on meta-research itself. A field with domain expertise in this exact failure, failing at the same rate as everyone else, would say something about how far knowing a problem gets you toward avoiding it.

Meta-research articles cite retracted work, after retraction, at a lower rate than a matched comparison of articles in the same journals and years.

What would falsify it. A rate ratio at or above 1. The direction is stated because the alternative is the interesting one.
Prior expectation. Nothing in the corpus estimates this, so the design has no anchor and does not pretend to one.

This is a better comparison than a fresh PubMed sample because it is drawn from the same query frame and differs on exactly the axis of interest.
Both arms require a reference list in PMC. Probe PA found 4948 of the cached articles carry one.

text:
The question
Meta-research tells other fields to share their data. It is a field defined by holding other research to a standard. The question is whether the papers doing that holding meet the standard themselves, and more precisely whether the ones arguing hardest for it are the ones most likely to meet it.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Hypothesis
A meta-research article whose own subject is data sharing, code sharing or research transparency carries a data availability statement, and a substantive one, more often than a meta-research article on any other subject.
The hypothesis is directional and it is the interesting direction. The null is that subject matter has no relationship with practice, which would mean advocacy and behavior are independent inside the one field where they should not be.
What would falsify it. An odds ratio whose confidence interval includes or falls below 1 for the transparency-topic coefficient, with the sample large enough to exclude an effect worth caring about. That result is publishable and would be the more striking of the two.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Unit of analysis
One meta-research article. 1088 of the 1830 records in the corpus carry a PMCID and therefore have retrievable full text. The remaining 742 are excluded and the exclusion is reported, because open-access availability is itself correlated with transparency practice and this biases the sample toward the transparent. That bias works against the null and has to be stated as a limitation rather than adjusted away.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Exposure and outcome
Exposure. The datashare topic label already derived for every record in build/lit/describe.py, which matches data sharing, code availability, FAIR and data reuse vocabulary against title, abstract and keywords. 84 records carry it.
Outcome. Presence and content of a data availability statement in the full text, taken from the JATS <sec sec-type="data-availability"> element. A pilot on three records found the element present in all three, so the extraction is not hypothetical. Statements are then graded on a three-level scale, because “data are available on request” and a repository accession are not the same claim:







level
meaning




none
no statement


declarative
a statement that shares nothing: on request, within the article, not applicable


actionable
a repository name, accession, DOI or URL that resolves



Grading the middle and top levels is done by rule on the statement text, and a random 100 statements are graded by hand to measure where the rule disagrees. The rule is not adjusted after seeing the outcome.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Analysis
In R. Logistic regression of an actionable statement on the transparency topic label, adjusted for publication year, journal and article type, with journal as a random effect because a journal’s own policy is the dominant driver of whether any statement appears at all and a fixed effect on 400 journals will not estimate.
glmer(actionable ~ topic_datashare + year_c + pubtype +
        (1 | journal), family = binomial, data = d)
An ordinal model on the three-level outcome is fitted alongside as the preregistered secondary, not as a fallback if the binary result disappoints.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Novelty
This is not a transparency-of-X study with X swapped, and the distinction is the reason the proposal exists. Sofi-Mahmudi and colleagues measured the transparency of COVID-19 research (PMID 37494359) and the FAIRness of its data (PMID 39556553); both estimate a rate in a population. A 2026 study measured data availability statements in dentistry journals (PMID 41955959) and is again a rate.
This asks whether one measurable property of a paper predicts another property of the same paper. It has an exposure, an outcome and a direction, and it can come out the other way.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
What it costs
1088 PMC full-text fetches at the NCBI throttle, roughly twelve minutes, cached. The corpus is already harvested. No paid service and no API key.

title: Does advocating transparency predict practicing it?
text:
Known threats to the result

Journal policy confounds everything. A journal that mandates a statement produces one regardless of the author’s convictions. The random effect absorbs the average journal, not an interaction between journal policy and topic, and the estimate is within-journal only where a journal publishes both kinds of paper.
The exposure is a vocabulary match, not a judgment. A paper labelled datashare may mention data sharing once in passing. Misclassification here is non-differential with respect to the outcome and biases toward the null, which weakens a positive finding and strengthens a negative one.
60 percent PMC coverage is not random. Stated above; not fixable within this design.

text: Each result links back to the protocol it was run from, which was published first and is unchanged. A result page reports what the analysis found and every defect found while running it, including the ones that changed the answer.

title: Results
section: Defects are part of the result
text:
Defects are part of the result
Every study here reports the bugs found during its own run, what each one cost, and which direction the correction moved the estimate. That is not modesty. Generated analysis code fails silently: it produces a number rather than an error, and the number is plausible. The first study found two such defects, one of which was inflating its own effect through an artifact and one of which was suppressing it.
A result published without that section is a result whose checks either were not run or were not reported, and neither is a reason to trust it more.

title: Results
text:
Review
No result here has been reviewed. Review is by two models from different providers, each instructed to refute the study, and no study is reviewed by one model alone. The second reviewer’s quota resets on 2026-09-20.
The protocols were published before the analyses ran, which is the property that matters most and is preserved regardless of when review happens: the analysis could not redefine its own question after seeing the answer.

title: The agenda
text:
Each proposal below is a protocol. It states a hypothesis, what would falsify it, the unit of analysis, the data source with a call that proved the source reachable, and the analysis in R, and it is published in that state before any analysis is run.
The order matters and it is deliberate. A protocol written after the result is known is not a protocol, and a project that criticizes selective reporting cannot itself decide what its question was once it has seen the answer. Every proposal therefore carries a date and a status, and a result page will link back to the protocol as it stood.

title: The agenda

Status values
The distinction between a design and a protocol is not cosmetic. It comes from the sibling project’s design standard and it is the rule this project works to: the difference between a design and a protocol is a set of computed numbers. A document that asserts its sample size, its power or its feasibility rather than measuring them is a design, whatever it calls itself.
Every document from P10 onward is written against this project’s own design standard, twelve requirements each traced to the review finding that produced it.

Where each one stands
